title: China's Economic Peak Has Passed: Credit Dries Up, Deflation Looms
dek: China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has been declining since; credit growth has fallen from 18% to 5%, and real growth may be only 1.5%-2%; the US has outperformed for five consecutive years. The narrative of industrial chain dominance is disproven by data; the future looks more like Japan-style deflation.
why: To counter the mainstream narrative that 'China's new industries = growth engine,' grounding judgments in verifiable data on credit, special bonds, and demographics; for those who want to update their long-term view of China-US relations.
who: Investors and researchers making China-US macro judgments, and business decision-makers treating China as a market or supply chain source; especially those wanting to test the 'China's new industries = growth engine' narrative.
skip: The first 3 minutes of guest introduction and article preamble can be skipped; start listening from the data comparison at 1:16.

points.h: China has missed its window to overtake the US
points.body: Dmitri sets the tone with official data: China's share of global GDP peaked at 18.5% in 2021 and has declined each year since; the US has risen from 24% to about 26%. He concludes that China has almost no chance of replacing the US as the world's largest economy, and the US economic advantage may continue to widen over the next decade. Logan fully agrees and steers the discussion toward a 'decline, not collapse' framework.

points.h: The root of China's slowdown is the end of credit expansion
points.body: Logan attributes China's slowdown to the end of extraordinary credit expansion. After the financial crisis, China added credit equivalent to one-third of global GDP in eight years; credit growth fell from an average of 18% in 2007-2016 to 9% after 2017, and now stands at just over 5%. Once credit stops, borrowers cannot refinance, and investment slows. Official figures still report 5.2% growth in 2023 and 5% in 2024 and 2025, but he estimates real growth since 2022 has been only 1.5%-2%, already below the US.

points.h: Using purchasing power parity rewards deflation
points.body: Addressing the common rebuttal that 'China has already surpassed the US in PPP terms,' Logan says PPP comparisons are meaningful for developing countries but untenable between the world's two largest economies: scoring by PPP rewards China for producing deflation—the lower domestic prices are, the stronger the economy appears, yet deflation is precisely the problem. He also stresses that debt is repaid in nominal local currency, so nominal GDP matters; the exchange rate is not an exogenous variable but an external signal of China's policy capacity.

points.h: Capital controls are not a cure, only a time-buyer
points.body: Logan acknowledges that China's capital controls are effective but argues they are not a panacea for massive macroeconomic imbalances. The impossible trinity dictates that free capital flow, exchange rate stability, and monetary policy independence can only be achieved two at a time. The function of capital controls is to delay outflows, suppress rapid cross-border volatility, and channel outflows into government-visible avenues—Huawei and BYD can go global aggressively, while private firms like HNA in 2016 had their overseas acquisitions halted; this is the two sides of the screening mechanism.

points.h: Credit still subsidizes old industries, not new ones
points.body: Logan rebuts the claim that 'credit is shifting to more productive new industries': central bank data shows that the share of loans issued at or below the Loan Prime Rate has risen from over 20% to 59%, indicating banks are continuously subsidizing. The share of special revenue bonds directed to so-called strategic industries rose only from about 2% in 2021 to 6% in 2025, with the vast majority still flowing to traditional sectors. Using the 2023 input-output table, he estimates that electric vehicles, batteries, AI, solar, etc., together account for about 6.3% of GDP, while the decline in real estate and infrastructure investment is about six times the increase in these new industries.

points.h: Europe is the last buyer of China's excess capacity
points.body: Logan judges that if Europe turns protectionist, China will be 'truly finished': the US market has narrowed and transshipment space is limited, and the developing world cannot absorb China's excess capacity while maintaining its own growth. He warns that the US is wrong to focus only on the bilateral deficit—the deficit is determined by the savings-investment gap; tariffs only redistribute the deficit, and not addressing the fundamental imbalance will only spawn more transshipment trade.

points.h: Without touching taxes, domestic demand won't pick up
points.body: Logan draws a parallel with Soviet Kosygin reforms: Brezhnev chose to pivot to a technological revolution rather than push reforms and maintain ideology. To convert savings into consumption, the real lever is tax policy—extracting resources from high-net-worth individuals, state-owned enterprises, and private firms excluded from the financial system. But he thinks it is almost inconceivable that Xi Jinping would go on TV to announce that 'the fiscal and financial system of the past 15 years will no longer apply in the future'; Beijing's insistence on the 5% growth narrative is partly to undermine export controls and dissuade Western investment in alternative supply chains.

points.h: China in 2035 will look like Japan today
points.body: Logan predicts that without major policy changes, China's economy in 2035 will resemble Japan's: persistent deflation, persistent external surpluses, exchange rate depreciation pressure, and low interest rates. The hardest constraint is demographics—China's actual average age at death is 73, and the early PRC baby boom will bring a population decline of 50-60 million over the next decade, about 3%-4% of the total population; even maintaining last year's low birth rate of 7.92 million won't stop it. He also reminds that the fiscal deficit is already close to $2 trillion per year, about 9.5% of GDP, leaving far fewer resources available than in the past. Finally, he says that if China truly wins by export share, it will invite stronger political backlash—'winning is losing.'

quotes.text: According to China's own economic data, which is chronically underreported, China peaked as a proportion of the global economy in 2021 at 18.5% of global GDP and has declined ever since.
China saw basically an expansion of around a third of global GDP in new credit in just eight years. And we've never seen anything like this.
China's financial system is a bunch of assets without markets for them.
it's not crisis or collapse, it's decay that you're seeing in terms of this pressure.
It doesn't have to be called a quote unquote financial crisis, but it has all the same consequences of a financial crisis.
